prompt: Match each Kinesis term from lesson 20 to its Kafka counterpart.
hint: One Kafka word on the right has no Kinesis counterpart here.

pairs.left: checkpoint kept by the Kinesis Client Library
pairs.right: committed offset of a consumer group

prompt: A topic has three partitions and the group `fraud` has two running members. How are the partitions read?
hint: Within a group, a partition has one reader.

choices.text: Both members read all three partitions, and each record is processed twice
choices.why: That is what two different groups do; members of one group share the partitions.

choices.text: One member reads two partitions and the other reads one
choices.why: Right. Each partition goes to exactly one member, and a rebalance moves them when a member joins or leaves.

choices.text: The members take records in turn from every partition
choices.why: Records of one partition are never split between members, or their order would be lost.

choices.text: Only one member reads; the other waits until the first one fails
choices.why: With three partitions and two members both get work; an idle member happens only when members outnumber partitions.

prompt: Quitanda raises a topic from 3 partitions to 4 while producers keep writing, and `c-17`, on partition 1 of 3, maps to partition 3 of 4. What happens to the order of its records?
hint: The partition is murmur2(key) modulo the partition count.

choices.text: Nothing: Kafka keeps the lineage, as Kinesis does after a reshard
choices.why: Kinesis records parents and children; Kafka keeps no lineage between partitions.

choices.text: Old and new records sit in two partitions, with no order between them
choices.why: Right. The modulus changed, and nothing links the two partitions, so a reader may see the new records first.

choices.text: Kafka moves `c-17`'s old records into the new partition
choices.why: Existing records never move between partitions.

choices.text: The topic refuses writes until consumers have read the old partitions
choices.why: Adding partitions does not pause producers.

prompt: What does a topic with `cleanup.policy=compact` keep?
hint: It turns a topic into something like a table.

choices.text: Every record for seven days, compressed
choices.why: Compaction is not compression; it is about keys.

choices.text: Only the records that no consumer group has read yet
choices.why: Kafka never deletes by what has been read.

choices.text: At least the latest record for every key
choices.why: Right: the current address of every customer, kept for as long as the topic exists.

prompt: `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` shows CURRENT-OFFSET 1 and LOG-END-OFFSET 2 for a partition. What is the lag, and what does it mean?

choices.text: 1: one record the group has not read
choices.why: Right. In the lab it was 1 on every partition after three more events were sent.

choices.text: 2: the group must read two more records before it is current
choices.why: The committed offset is the next one to read; 2 − 1 is one record.

choices.text: 3: the sum of the two numbers
choices.why: Lag is the difference between the end of the log and the committed offset.

choices.text: 1: one consumer is missing from the group to read it
choices.why: Lag counts records, not members.

prompt: The console consumer of the group `fraud` exited after reading four records. Three more were sent, and a new consumer in the same group was started without `--from-beginning`. What did it read?
hint: Where is the group's position kept?

choices.text: All seven, because a new process starts from the beginning
choices.why: The group's committed offsets are on the broker; a new member carries on from them.

choices.text: Nothing, because it starts at the end of the log
choices.why: That happens to a group with no committed offsets; this one had them.

choices.text: Exactly the three new records
choices.why: Right. It carried on from the offsets the group had committed.

choices.text: The four old records again, then the three new ones
choices.why: Replaying needs a reset of the group's offsets, which came later.

prompt: To make the group `fraud` read its topic again from the start, the lab ran `kafka-consumer-groups.sh` with `--reset-offsets --to-___ --execute`.
A topic has `retention.ms` of seven days. Why can a partition still hold a record that is eight days old?

choices.text: Retention counts from the moment the record was last read
choices.why: Reading changes nothing in Kafka's log.

choices.text: Retention deletes whole segments, and its segment also holds younger records
choices.why: Right. A segment goes only when all of it is past the limit.

choices.text: `retention.bytes` overrides `retention.ms` when both are set
choices.why: Whichever is reached first applies; neither keeps a record longer.

choices.text: A consumer group with lag holds the record back from deletion
choices.why: Kafka deletes regardless of lag; a group that falls behind loses records.

prompt: Creating a topic with replication factor 3 on the single broker failed. Why?
hint: Each copy lives on a different broker.

choices.text: Each copy needs its own broker, and there was one
choices.why: Right; the message said "only 1 broker(s) are registered".

choices.text: Kafka 4 dropped replication in favour of KRaft, its new metadata mode
choices.why: KRaft replaced ZooKeeper for metadata; replication of partitions is unchanged.

choices.text: The disk had no room for three copies
choices.why: The refusal was about brokers, not space.

choices.text: `min.insync.replicas` was 1
choices.why: That setting decides when writes are refused, not how many copies may exist.

prompt: Replication factor 3 across three zones, `acks=all`, and `min.insync.replicas` of 2. Two zones fail. What happens to writes?
hint: How many in-sync replicas are left?

choices.text: They continue on the one remaining copy
choices.why: That would accept writes on a single copy, which the setting of 2 exists to refuse.

choices.text: They are refused until a second replica is in sync again
choices.why: Right. With one in-sync replica left, below the minimum of 2, the partition stops taking writes rather than risk losing them.

choices.text: Kafka creates two new replicas in the surviving zone and carries on
choices.why: Kafka does not re-replicate on its own to restore the factor.

choices.text: Writes succeed, and the records are lost when the zones return
choices.why: The writes are not accepted in the first place.

prompt: Which of these are true of an MSK cluster? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what AWS manages from what stays yours, and what is billed.

choices.text: Traffic between its brokers for replication is not billed
choices.why: Right; AWS does not charge for it.

choices.text: A producer in one zone writing to a leader in another pays the zone-crossing price
choices.why: Right, in each direction.

choices.text: The replication factor of each topic is chosen by AWS and cannot be changed
choices.why: It is a Kafka setting and stays yours; MSK only sets defaults.

choices.text: The number of brokers is a multiple of the number of zones
choices.why: Right; MSK places them evenly.

prompt: moto answered `create-cluster` with `CREATING` and `describe-cluster` with a `ZookeeperConnectString` of `zookeeper.example.com:2181`. What can a program connect to?

choices.text: To `zookeeper.example.com:2181`, once the state reaches `ACTIVE`
choices.why: That host is a placeholder that does not exist, and the state never changes in moto.

choices.text: Nothing: moto runs no broker, and `get-bootstrap-brokers` failed with a 500
choices.why: Right. The MSK half of the lesson is the API's shape; the behaviour was seen on the local broker.

choices.text: To `localhost:9092`, where moto starts a broker for each cluster
choices.why: That port was the real Kafka of the earlier section, started by hand.

choices.text: To any of the three subnets given
choices.why: A subnet is not an address to connect to, and `subnet-a` is not even a subnet id.

prompt: Quitanda wants a topic kept for six months on a provisioned MSK cluster without buying large broker disks. What fits?
hint: Older segments can live somewhere other than the brokers.

choices.text: Tiered storage, which moves older segments off the brokers
choices.why: Right, at a lower price per GB. The brokers keep the recent part, and a long retention stops needing large disks.

choices.text: Lowering the brokers' storage after the topic is created, to keep costs down
choices.why: Broker storage can be raised and never lowered.

choices.text: `cleanup.policy=compact`
choices.why: Compaction keeps the latest record per key and drops the history six months asks for.

choices.text: MSK Serverless, which keeps records with no limit
choices.why: Serverless documents a cap on how long records are kept.

choices.text: A VPN between your datacentre and the cluster, for clients outside AWS
choices.why: That is Site-to-Site VPN, in `aws-foundations`; Connect moves data, not packets.

choices.text: Kafka Connect: connectors that move data in and out of Kafka
choices.why: Right: a database's change log into a topic, or a topic into S3.

choices.text: The brokers' KRaft controllers, which keep the cluster's metadata
choices.why: MSK runs those in every cluster; Connect is a separate service.

prompt: For 20 GB a day, the provisioned MSK cluster cost 850.41 a month and Kinesis 170.10. What makes the difference?
hint: Which line is there before a byte is written?

choices.text: MSK charges three times for every record because of replication
choices.why: Replication traffic is not billed; the three copies cost disk, which is 114.00 of it.

choices.text: The zone-crossing traffic
choices.why: That line was 24.00.

choices.text: The brokers: 712.41 a month whatever the traffic
choices.why: Right. At 20 GB a day they carry a small fraction of what they could.

choices.text: Kinesis retention is free for seven days
choices.why: Seven days cost 87.60 on the Kinesis side.

prompt: Suppose Kinesis costs 8.51 per GB a day of traffic and nothing fixed, and the MSK cluster 712.41 fixed plus 6.90 per GB a day. At how many GB a day do they cost the same? Round to the nearest whole number.
Which situation argues for MSK even at Quitanda's modest volume?
hint: Price is not the only column of the comparison.

choices.text: The team wants no servers to look after
choices.why: That argues for Kinesis, which has no brokers.

choices.text: A fraud check needs each order's events in order
choices.why: Both order per key; Kinesis does it per shard.

choices.text: The consumers are Lambda functions and a Firehose copy to S3
choices.why: Those are AWS's own integrations, and they sit with Kinesis.

choices.text: Services already written for Kafka clients and Connect
choices.why: Right. Kafka itself is the requirement, and rewriting them for Kinesis costs more than the brokers.

prompt: Put in order the steps of running and reading the local Kafka broker of this lesson.
hint: Nothing can be created before the broker runs, and it cannot run unformatted.
items: Format the log directory with a cluster id
Create the topic `orders` with three partitions
Send keyed records with the console producer
Read them in the group `fraud` and describe its lag

prompt: Which retention can Kafka offer that Kinesis Data Streams cannot?
hint: Kinesis expires records by age, up to a year.

choices.text: A retention of seven days
choices.why: Kinesis keeps up to 365 days, seven included.

choices.text: The latest record per key, kept for as long as the topic exists
choices.why: Right: compaction, which Kinesis has no equivalent of.

choices.text: A retention of 24 hours
choices.why: That is Kinesis's default.

choices.text: Retention that waits until every group has read a record
choices.why: Neither deletes by what was read.
